T1: Set the goal, the countries of interest and the bar: make sure the citizens are accurate, and say how that is checked.
Researched the evidence and datasets with three helper agents, wrote the measurement plan and country recommendation, built the first code and ran baselines on real data.
T2: Questioned the need for a paid key, proposed testing on public data first, and offered browser access for downloads.
Stood in for the model with blind predictions, downloaded the World Values Survey with a headless browser, and stress-tested the US, Singapore and China.
T3: Set the bar: make it work instead of regressing to the average.
Tested five remedies; three failed and anchoring citizens to real survey records worked.
T4: Asked for simpler explanations six times.
Rewrote explanations with analogies and worked examples.
T5: Asked to see the gains and for more data; proposed local data weighted Bayesian-style, like superforecasting.
Built the first scorecard page, downloaded all 62 countries, and built pooling that weighs each source by its track record.
T6: Proposed using news, social media, reports and research.
Combed sources with two helper agents, turned 96 published findings into evidence and tested them: little value.
T7: Set out the conditions, built and ran the US test, and found and corrected an earlier scoring error of mine.
T8: Asked for one simple table, proposed building it around the one-line summary, drew the budget implication and banned jargon.
Built the tables, defined points off, and replaced jargon with agreed plain terms.
T9: Spotted that filling in groups is itself AI, checked understanding, and asked to show the US against Singapore.
Wrote the two-kinds explanation, the two-women example and the US-versus-Singapore chart.
T10: Asked for a streamlined page and flagged text that was hard to grasp.
Rebuilt the page around what AI can and cannot do, with one example person.
T11: Challenged the framing of a result and asked why the US had not been tested.
Reframed against the no-AI baseline and ran the missing US test.
T12: Reviewed the page with screenshots and set wording and layout changes.
Rewrote the one-line result, explanations and terms; replaced negative wording.
T13: Tested own understanding, asked for guidance on when to use AI, and insisted on the agreed language.
Framed results as error removed and wrote the when-to-use guide in agreed terms.
T14: Questioned claims and sources: an untested claim, a group example, a figure's source, survey timing.
Rechecked the data, removed or corrected claims, and found the survey's fieldwork dates.
T15: Reviewed the page section by section with screenshots and drafted wording.
Rebuilt the page flow so terms are defined first; rewrote tables, chart and explanations.
T16: Specified the five rules and chose section titles.
Checked every number in the rules, designed the split-sample pilot and rewrote the limits.
T17: Asked for a thorough QA and this record.
Ran QA with an independent helper agent, fixed findings, wrote this page and the reusable package.
T18: Checked the conclusion, added the small-groups line, asked what the blend meant, and challenged the mixed methods.
Ran one test for every number, found the chatbot blend and the standout-groups claim did not hold, and rebuilt the page and package from it.
T19: Asked for alternative methods, then chose three to test: a panel of chatbots, fewer standard questions, boosting small groups.
Ran the three tests on the one-method design, with blind predictions from four more models, and wrote them up with 95% ranges.
T20: Asked whether a claim was backed by evidence, what reading records through a paid key involves and costs, and to add the figures to both pages.
Checked the claim against the source paper and our own data, measured how much group answers move, priced the next test, and updated both pages.
T21: Asked whether individuals need to be asked repeatedly, then asked for a thorough QA and a smoother, more accessible scorecard.
Answered from the data, reordered and tightened the page, ran independent number and accessibility reviews, and fixed every finding.
T22: Asked whether "combination" means blended and how to make it easy to grasp; proposed two visuals: the experiments behind the conclusions, and a decision tree.
Explained the blend with real shares and a data-driven box, then built the decision tree and evidence map on the scorecard and a timeline of every test in the casebook.
T23: Said the page had become too long and hard to follow for readers without a stats or tech background, and asked for a simpler flow with the same detail.
Rebuilt the page in layers with a worked example, and tested it on five fresh readers playing a non-technical executive, fixing what each one tripped on.

tests.title: Baselines
tests.asked: How close do simple rules get, with no AI?
tests.found: Last wave's answers, the average of other countries and demographics alone set the bar any AI has to beat.

tests.title: Chatbot stress test
tests.asked: Can a chatbot give each group's answers blind?
tests.found: It reproduced 81% of the real differences between groups in the US, but only 36% in Singapore and 25% in China: groups came out too alike.

tests.title: Five fixes for flattening
tests.asked: Can the chatbot's flat answers be fixed?
tests.found: Stretching its differences, sharpening its answers and showing it real answers first did not help (still about 5 points off in Singapore). Building citizens from real survey records did.
tests.changed: Record citizens; the other fixes dropped

tests.title: Learning from more countries
tests.asked: Does learning from more countries help?
tests.found: Record citizens learned from 61 other countries, about 90,000 people, were more accurate than from 2: 3.7 against 4.2 points off.
tests.changed: Record citizens learn from many countries

tests.title: Weighing sources by track record
tests.asked: King's superforecasting idea: should each source count by how accurate it has been?
tests.found: Yes. Record citizens earned about three times the chatbot's weight.

tests.title: Published findings as evidence
tests.asked: King's idea: do news, reports and research add anything?
tests.found: 96 published findings on Singapore were 8 points off on their own and did not improve the estimates.

tests.title: The survey library
tests.asked: King's idea: can we borrow the most similar question from another survey?
tests.found: Typically 11 points off, and about 9 even where the wording was near-identical.

tests.title: Small surveys, scored honestly
tests.asked: Was our first small-survey result right?
tests.found: No: people were checked against themselves, so 300 looked like 1,500. Redone honestly, 300 real people plus record citizens were about as accurate for each group as 600 without AI.

tests.title: The United States, like for like
tests.asked: King asked why the US had not been tested.
tests.found: Starting from the real overall answer, record citizens filled in US groups more closely than the chatbot: 1.8 against 2.3 points off.

tests.title: Which groups stand out
tests.asked: Which groups' answers sit furthest from the average?
tests.found: Indian and Malay Singaporeans and young adults in Singapore; Republicans, Democrats and Black Americans in the US.

tests.title: Independent audit
tests.asked: Does every number on the page hold up?
tests.found: The "standout groups" figures were really averages over all groups. Redone, the chatbot kind did not help most groups in Singapore.

tests.title: One method for everything
tests.asked: King noticed the page mixed setups.
tests.found: One test now produces every headline number. AI still makes a survey about twice as valuable, the gain is biggest for small groups, and which AI to add depends on whether the question has been asked before.
tests.changed: Every headline number; Rule 2 (QA findings 47 to 66)

tests.title: Three more ideas
tests.asked: King chose three ways to make AI more accurate.
tests.found: Five chatbots helped only when each was counted by its track record, then about as much as the best one. About 20 standard questions kept most of the benefit of 76. Extra people from small groups helped them about a point when read alone, less with AI.

tests.title: How consistent people are
tests.asked: King asked whether "people don't fully agree with themselves" was backed by evidence.
tests.found: People repeat 69% (our check) to 81% (Stanford study) of their answers weeks later, but a typical group's answers move only 1.7 points.
tests.changed: Score groups, not individuals (QA findings 69 to 72)

tests.title: Streamlining and a third audit
tests.asked: King asked for a thorough QA and a smoother page.
tests.found: No number was wrong, but the short answer overstated record citizens: for a brand-new question the two kinds of AI did about as well as each other.
